The Church has had its National Mission of Repentance and Hope. Hope springs eternal in the human breast, and the why and where- fore of it all is summarised by an old friend of mine—or" was, for many years have passed since he thus put the ancient story in a nutshell:— Pandora, the Eve of Grecian mythology, so named because she was the "all-gifted," having received from each of the gods in turn some power by which she might work the ruin of man, became the wife of ypimetheus. In her husband's house there was a closed box which she had forbidden him. to open. Moved by an irresistible curiosity, Epimetheus dared to open the box. All the ills that flesh is heir to there- upow-ponred out. Yet Pandora managed to shut down the lid and prevent the escape of Hope! Watts writes of Hope as getting music out of its lyre when all else has failed. Poke and poets generally bid us hope on and hope ever. Confessions. •

"I love little Pope," suddenly exclaimed an old tramp whom I accompanied along the road a little way • (as the reader may have more .than suspected long ,befor now, T have la weakness for disreputable cempany), and he treated me to an apt quotation from his favourite poet. Another of the fraternity confided to me that he had reached the allotted span, and had spent forty of his three score.and ten years in gaol! He was a merry, old soul, too, and could spin a good yarn. Another of these ne'er-do-wells I had known as curate in a country parish. He became a sad wreck—drink, of course—and used to bring me dirty MSS. of original sketches in exchange for the wherewithal to minister to his depraved appetite. He made his,home inn common lodging-house, and, though a scholar whose attainments one might well envy, apparently preferred that sort of life. Once I asked him if he had no, regrets, and he pre- tended that if it might all be lived over again, with full knowledge, the, conditions in which he found himself would be his deliberate choice! .

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST,
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST,
The Poetasters.

"Vigilant jocularly affected to deplore the Mayor's temporary lapse into rhyme at last week's C,ouneil meeting, but, as ,compared with the deliberate and persistent if unconscious offences of certain who are habitually given to that sort of thing,. his , Worship's fault was venial indeed. ' These worthy- but exceedingly troublesome folk exist in every district, regu- larly haunt the offices of the local Press, and are the despair of the ,editor. They .are so per- fectly tame and mild-mannered, and yet so in- ordinately conceited and blind to the truth so far as their pitiable verses are concerned, that they are by far the most difficult class to deal with. Twice or thrice have caught myself in this column dropping into—you know: a Is, Wegg—hut I was familiar with the alarming symptoms, and I pulled up before there was time for serious developments. Assuredly ap- preciative readers will be ready to testify out of full and grateful hearts .that,. while in ‘these notes I have repeatedly done the things I ought not to have done and have left undone the things I ought to have done, many nioomi' have waxed and waned since last I was betrayed into even a small offence of the kind now depre- cated. • An Awful Example. ~

In one town in which I had my headquarters some years, there dwelt a perfectly hopeless scribbler of the class referred to who, unfortun- ately as I always thought, was of independent means, and seemed to me to spend the whole of his time in producing incredible rubbish which he evidently .believed to be high-class poetry. Ile would call two or three times a week and inflict on me his latest folly, and for a while I submitted and endured with lamblike meekness. ventually my unsuspecting perse- cutor actually began to bring his worse than waste paper on publishing nights. Then I had to be positively rude—there was no alternative. Once when he was about' due, I slipped into another room and went on with my work, being exceptionally busy. Mine enemy found me, however. To my dismay. he walked to the fire- place, turned his back thereto, gathered up his coat-tails, and, holding. these in one Ifand and a formidable manuseript in the other, began to drivel in the old exasperating way. "Stop," I exclaimed, " and get oat of this. I've come here in hope of escape from such terrible bores as you." I was goaded to it; -desperate diseaies require desperate retoedies, and I had no more nonsense :from that quarter. - Now, -as Jack Bunsby' would 'say, the 'bearing of -these observations lies in the application. Let the ambitious versifier obtain the candid opinion of some competent friend, as to its merits before.worrying a polite and long-suffer- ing editor into printing stuff likely to make a laughing-stock of the author. Why This Thusness?

In Lymm notes " Critic " last week had occa- sion to refer to a lady's singing of "Annie Laurie." Why is that nonular song invariably sung in public by one of that sex? Surely any- one who calmly studies the work.will,agree that it is really a man's song, and that its exclusive appropriation by the ladies is duo to a little misapprehension at some time or other in the rather remote past.

The debt amounting to, £BO, which was owing ' by the Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Trust, has been completely liquidated • liy the generosity of Mr. William-Summerfield, and .both Chapel and school are now free from that incunibrance. In order to celebrate this happy event, thC mem- bers and congregation of the Church -held a .seei4l in the schoolroom on Saturday evening, tlfeehief guest' being Mr. William Summerfield.

The chair was occupied by the Rev. W. T. Derry, the. superintendent of the, circuit, who congratulated the members a the church upon the fact that they were now out of debt, a fact which was almost unique amongst Wesleyan bodies. The Rev: John Gunnell gave an his- torical sketch of the church at Sankey Bridges. He said the cause there commenced in a small way, by cottage services in the ola Vost Office. In 1876 a corrugated iron chapel was erected on the present site, and in 1885 the existing chapel was built, followed in 1892 by the schoolroom. He paid a tribute to the late Mr. William Summerfield, the father of their present guest, who for ten or twelve years was the caretaker of the chapel Without fee or reward. After Mr. Gunnell, a number Of local members of the church also spoke in high terms of Mr. Summer- field and the, Summerfield family generally. A musical programme was subsequently given, in which Mrs. J. Jones, Miss Moores and Mr. .George Gough gave solos, Mr. Levi Richardson being the accompanist. 7Master Sidney Parr also gave a pianoforte solo.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 18, 1916.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 18, 1916.
HIS WORSHIP WORSHIPS.
Picturesque Spectacle On Mayoral Sunday.

Wishing to"obtain a fresh point of view and also to satirise' the pomp and splendour of the London Lord Mayor's Day some years ago, an enterprising American ink imp engaged an old nag and a frowsy cab and, from the inside, re- corded the impression on the populace as his vehiclb rumbled along at the tail of the official procession. Last Sunday's Mayoral procession was no occasion for that. As far as the authorities were concerned it was just a simple and devout assembly moving to the Parish Church in% recognition of the connection between the Church and the Borough; made picturesque and inspiring by the dovetailing of brass bugle bands and companies of Firemen, Volunteers, Special Constables, Friendly Society representatives, Church Lads' Brigades and Boy Scouts. It was one of the longest proceSsions of recent years, and commensurate both 'with the dignity of Mayoral Sunday and particularly as an ex- pression of sucipOrt, to our war-time Mayor, Alderman Peter --Peacock. So extended was it that, without councillors, magistrates, and other public men, it covered the drive round the lawn in front 'of the Town 'Hall. - . The band of the R.A.0.8. (in charge of Mr. IL Smith), led the way followed by the War- rington Company of the V.T.C. (in command of Captain W. P. Rylands), the Stockton Heath Detachment of the V.T.C. (Lieut. Frank War- burton), Church Lads' Cadet_Battalien (Capt. J.. A. Brookes), Grammar School Cadet Corps (Captain Pearson), Boy Scouts—all given the salute as they passed the Mayor—St. John Ambulance Brigade, Tire Brigade and Police Force, including about t,eventy "Specials." Then came the sword and mace bearers, who heralded the immediate approaCh of the Mayor, who walked with Alderman Smethurst and the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle). And then aldermen, councillors magistrates, officials, Education Comr.ittee, Education officials, non-inembers of the Council, Board of Guardians, Board of Management of Infirmary, Insurance Committee, townsmen and Friendly Societies, the duties of chief I marshal for the last-named being discharged by Bro. T. P. Bradshaw, P.P.G.M., Independent Order of Oddfellows (Manchester 'Unity). Among the prominent ladies and gentlemen present were: Aldermen Tinnion, Bennett, Councillors Diekenson, -Henshall, Cliantler, Dale, Cunnington, Lindley, Halliwell, Broad- hurst, Chrimes, Lashford, J. T. Locker, Messrs. J. W. Ifayward,,,J. Bailey, S. Wright, G. F. White, W. Furness, A. J. Jolley, W. Daintith, J. H. Smethurst, George Walker, H. Collin, It. Cook, W. E. Stout, J. H. J. Hampson, S. Brocklehurst, W. Bibby, J. F. Forster, F. Dickens, P. Delaney, A. Tilling, Mrs. Hall and Mrs. Bell. Lieut.-Colonel-Lyon and Lieut.- Colonel Mocntta wero pre*nt at the church. • Rector On Real Unity. In the course of his sermon "the Mayor's Chaplain (the Rev. Canon Willis) said he be- lieved that, under God, owing to the war, there had been and would be great blessing to the nation and the world. Real unity was spread- ing amongst the nation, and there. was a re- vival; he hoped, of real religion, not of mere form and ceremony. He trusted that eventually there would be peace, but it could' not be so until the enemy had been conquered, for that would mean no true and lasting peace at all. And then. he hoped, by having a league of all the nations, war would become an impossibility, and prosperity and happiness would ensue. On the procession returning to the Town Hall the various bodies were :dismissed with the thanks of the Mayor for their attendance, and the leaders entered , the Council Chamber, where the health of his Worship was drunk, on the proposition of Alderman Smethurst.

div.head: AT THE BAPTIST CHURCH.
div.p: AT THE BAPTIST CHURCH.

On Monday evening his Worship the Mayor with sword and mace bearers, attended divine service at Crolbo'rne-street Baptist Church. The Special Constables of the town were also in- vited,.and about fifty were present. The Rev. IL Ogden, pastor,- is himself-a Special Constable, and the only minister amongst that body. He preached from the text, Matthew v., 25, and on the subject, "Law prevents war," pointing out that as in the case -of man's development from savagery, law became necessary for the-punish- ment of individuals, so international law should be used for the purpose of restr4lnt and punish- ment in the case of nations.

div.head: LADY VISITORS.
div.p: LADY VISITORS.
Scheme Which Will Please Whitecross Hospital Soldiers.

With the object of making the lives of the soldiers at Whitecross Hospital brighter and happier by visiting them, a meeting was held at the Workhouse on Tuesday morning for the purpose of forming a Ladies' Visiting Corn: mittee. The Idea is that the ladies should form themselves into sections, each section to take a ward under their care.

Mr. A. J. Jolley presided, and there were also present Mr. W. Furness and Mr. A. Bottomley (clerk) 'and the following ladies:-- Mesdames A. J. Willett, J. Dodds, J. T. Locker, Downham, Bracecamp, Bottortiley, Hodgkinson, W. Furness, Lindley, T. Locker, Hulme, Smith, R. Timsais, C. E. Parker, 'Davies, Bowden, T. A. Murray, F. Booth, E. Aubrey White, E. Bradshaw,' Fred Short, Kipps, Miss Broadbent and Miss E. A. Birchall.

The Chairman announced that the Mayoress was unable to be present owing to a severe cold. Referring to the proposed new scheme, he said it would be .on the lines of the one now in operation at the Lord Derby War Hospital, where a body of lady visitors were working. At the Whitecross Hospital they had been able, up till now,to provide small comforts, and arrange in various little mays, to increase the comfort and happiness of the men. That had been done by 'a 'small -body -of voluntary workers, who had given their time very freely. The numbers in the hospital, however, bad, now grown to such an unexpected extent—and -they were shortly to be increased still further—that they thought something must be done on more organised lines. Some months ago the Mayoress herself suggested that if something of this kind could be done, she would be pleased to do everything in her power to assist it. The suggested pro- gramme was that the ladies should visit the blocks of buildings which were in occupation as a military hospital, and also the blocks which would shortly be put to such a use, and see for themselves, so that they might decide on such a procedure to carry out the work for the com- fort of the men.

div.head: Men to Co-operate.
div.p: The Men to Co-operate.

A successful plan would be to invite the co- operation of the men themselves. A few weeks ago ‘a committee was started for the providing of concerts for the men, and. any co-operation in that direction would be, welcome. A comforts' fund had been started, and would be all the better for being replenished. • Bottomley said that the arrangement was that the ladies present, in co-operatio4 with their- friends, should act as lady visitors, each taking certain sections of ' the hospital. He pointed out that at the present time, as there was not a xesident medical officer 'at the 'hos- pital, the cases were not as serious as in the first instance. But +her were making arrangements for a further two hundred patients, and they -were bound to have, a fully-qualified resident 'medical officer. They would get different classes of patients, and there would be a lot of work for the ladies to do. Visits from the ladies would be heartily welcomed by the men.'

div.head: Handicraft Work Recommended.
div.p: Handicraft Work Recommended.

Miss Margaret Broadbent suggested that the men be shown handicrafts and fancy work. She could assure the ladies that, from her experience at Raddon Court, the men took quickly to th'e work, and there was no. difficulty in disposing of it.

In reply to a question by one of the ladies, the Chairman replied that it was not intended that the ladies should pledge themselves to different visiting days. • Tho ladies-ithen visited the hospital, and after obtaining an insight into, the work which con- fronted them, returned to the Board-room.

Mrs. Parker took the chair, in the absence of the Mayoress, and it was decided that a meet- ing be held next Tuesday to discuss the work, elect wards, fix visiting days, and choose a com- mittee. The question wa's raised as to whether a secretary would be needed, but Mr. Bottomiev said he would attend the meetings and do all he could for The ladies.

div.head: PROBLEM ,OF LIFE.
div.p: PROBLEM ,OF LIFE.
Might Is Right In Nature, Says Dr. Naden.
QUESTIONS OF MORALS.

Dr. J. B. Naden addressed the members of the Literary and Philosophical Society on Monday evening on." The Problem of Life," the subject. having been suggested to him by the remark of a lady, who was impatient of the difference be- tween ideals and their realisation, "Oh, we are all wrongly made."

The sentiment was Often felt and -sometimes expressed of the world in general, he said. ' Would not we shatter it to bits, and then re- mould it to the heart's desire? Were such sen- timents reasonable? In. some instances they led to a sighing acquiescence in the inevitable. The world was made on a wrong plan, it could not be altered, and we must make the best of it. In others they led to despair 'and gloomy doubt of the worth of anything and everything—a state of mind only to be relieved by faith in a better world to come, in which the ills of this life would be compensated and redressed. Although many questions rem.ained unanswered, we had some rogh idea now how things had cerae to be ai they-are.' We knew that higher forms of life had slowly evolved 11.61111(4er, and that Nature had not been squeamish about her methods. Woe to the conquered! "Might is right" had been her principle. With very slight, but important, modifications, it was so still. All forms of life were dependent on other :fornis, -living or 'dead, for food—there were all the elements to produce an everlasting row. (Laughter). Although man was the lord of creation, 'his •dominion was incomplete and his supposed vassals frequently exercised their rights to his discomfort and annoyance. Dr. •Naden.-instanced the toll taken by great beasts, snakes, &c., insect life and parasites, and micro- scopic flora and fauna.

div.head: World not Freak of Madness.
div.p: World not Freak of Madness.

on the question of morals he alleged that our ideals were far in advance of our inclinations. We watched lambs at play on a hillock and thought it a shame they should be sacrificed, but it did not seriously interfere with our satis- faction when the joint appeared on the table. (Laughter.) Public morals were higher than the snin of individual- consciences. The lecturer quoted a number of interesting views of life by poets and .philosophers, includ-. ing Carlyle's, who, on looking at the midnight stars, said it was a sad sight, as he thought there might be many more worlds as: bad as ours. It was easy—too easy—to feel this sombre side of life. But there must be anbther side if we cared to look for it, an let it play on our minds and feelings. "I cannot believe," said Naden, "that a glorious world like this, which appeals at once •to artistic, intellectual Dnimal pgwers, it; a mere ak of madness." He went on to shy that the ultimate purpose of life was happiness for the individu,al, animal, or plant, and if that purpose were not on the whole fulfilled then life was a failure. Dealing with progress, he was of opinion that its real benefit was spiritual. A profit and loss account of progress might not be what we imagined, but he had little doubt there would be a balaiice on .the credit side, and the heaviest item would not be our material prosperity, but the enlarged outlook of the human mind. _ _

The lecturer having dealt at no little length with the cellular theory, pointed out that for the existence of an advanced And varied fauna the destruction of life was absolutely necessary for food. Harking back to the question of morals, which was also discussed fully, the speaker apparently came to the conclusion that "man's position might be desmibed as a little higher than the brutes and rather more than a little lower than the angels. There was a wide gap between ideals and their realisations. Personal desire and personal self-tesertion must yield to the impersonal, indifferent and un- alterable powers of the world. In only a very limited sense were we masters of our fate.'

div.head: WORLD OF W:STERY.
div.p: A WORLD OF W:STERY.

Mr. Rymer Young, who proposed a vote of thanks to Dr..Naden, said that the present war was calculated to shake a man in his ideas. When they saw the lives lost and the homes ruined by the war they were inclined to ask what kind of happiness was going to come out of all this. Any happiness to be proportionate to the suffering would be a heaven on earth. Mr. L. Greening said that wheg he was twenty years of age he thought he knew exactly what life was; at forty he had his doubts as to whether his ideas were correct; and at sixty he now admitted- that he did not know what life was. (Laughter.) • He had realised, however, that there' was an object in • life—that we should live for the benefit of the trace and not the individual. Mr. A. J. Jolley, while recognising the -literary value of the paper, thought that as regards its philosophical value there was more room for opinion. He did not agree that men should be looked at as merely being a little above the ..brute level, and ,he did not think it was' quite right to trace it development in lower forms in what we regarded as moral sentiment and feeling. He again joined issue With the lecturer, who said that progress was stow. An enormous distance separated us from our grandfathers and things had =iced very quickly even within the last quarter of a century. Mr. 0. Lofthouse put forward the view that moral and spiritual development was necessary in solving the problem.

div.head: STRANGE FIRE INCIDENT.
div.p: STRANGE FIRE INCIDENT.
Bags Of Sand As Extinguishers
At Gas Works.
At 5.30 on Wednesday evening a fire of an imusual character broke out in the fitting de- partment of the Longford Gas Works, Winwick- road.

So far as can be ascertained, the PreSSUre of gas New out a piece•of inch and a half piping connecting the meter and the largest, main; and the gas, becoming ignited, threw out a flame about twenty feet in length. It was a startling occurrence, and one man was slightly injured. .The employes were unable to extinguish the fire, which, owing to its 'situation, might have had alarming results. _ _

The Fire Brigade was summoned and, a. full comylement of men turned out under Deputy- Superintendent H. Cook Water was of little service, nd the difficulty was effectually solved by the use of many barrow-loads of sand, which were hurled against the flame. After an hour's hard work the fire was smothered and further danger averted. , The outbreak was hard to locate sufficiently, having taken place under- neath, but smart work and efficient service by the brigade saved the premises. •

div.head: STY:ICELAND.
div.p: STY:ICELAND.
Royal Court.

"Tiger's Cub," now being presented at the Royal Court Theatre, is an interesting play with an Alaskan_setting, and wit, which has the virility and sparkle of the adventurous American temperament. It has the advantage of being played by a first-class company. With it is Mr. Sam Livesey, who left London three weeks ago to take up the, part of Bill Slark, whose previous interpreter has just joined the Army. Mr. Livesey knows how " Tiger's Cub" should be presented, for it was he who created the part of the Tiger when the play had its successful initiation at the Garrick. Theatre, London.

Mr. Livesey has had an interesting theatrical career. div.p: TEMPERANCE SUNDAY.,
Can The Christian Churches Master The Drink Traffic ?
COURAGEOUS ACTION
NEEDED.

At a largely attended public meeting held in the Co-operative Hall, Warrington, on Sunday evening a resolution was adopted calltrig upon His Majesty's Government to deal drastically with .the -liquor traffic -without delay. Mrs. James Dodds, President of the War- rington Band of Hope Union, presided. It was a matter for thankfulness, she said, to be spared to see another anniversary. div.p: TEMPERANCE COUNCIL DEMANDS.

The Rev. A. Leathley Heap (Leeds) delivered an address, in the course of which he said he thought he might say we are all temperance reformers now. The facts of the war had brought home to the mind of the people the terrible evil of drink and the desire to do something to slay its ravages and its weaken-. ing power. He referred to the movement dur- ing the past year in favour of prohibition or nationalisation, and to the very helpful results which had -followed the -work-of the Central Board of Liquor Control. Drink, he said, is still a terrible•power—an enemy causing enor- mous waste, weakening the power of the workers - and increasing infantile mortality. We needed—in order to secure the nation in. future—a healthy, promising child population, and we should safeguard child-life in, every possible form. Speaking of the recently formed Temperance Council of the Christian Churches, he said: "If the Christian Churches nre strong enough and courageous enough we can master the drink traffic. Our hope is in the , Christian Church." (Loud applause.) This Temperance Council was, he explained, fully in agreement upon the following nine points:—(l) Sunday closing; (2) Restriction of the hours of the sale of drink on week-days; (3) Reduction of the number of licensed pre- mises; (4) Increase in the power of local Licensing Authorities; (5) Control of clubs; (6) Abolition of grocers' licences; (7) Prohibi- tion of the sale of intoxicating-liquor to young persons; (8) Local option; and ~(9) Provision of alternatives to the liquor traffic. PeAonally he was prepared to consider any measure that would lessen the evil. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: IMMORTALITY.
div.p: IMMORTALITY.
Shan We Know Our Dead Again?

The Rev. T. T. James„eontinuing his series 0, sermons on "God .and the war" at Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday,- spoke on the theme, a Shall we know our dead again?" The question regarding immortality, he saidc rises again and again in the human mind— whether we can reasonably look forward to a recognition of each other in another life, whether we can expect to know and recognise those who have preceded us or come after us across the border. Of course, all this amounted to the question whether personal consciousness continues beyond the Gate of Death. Immortality was a very broad term and had been made to stand for widely different ideas. There was that view which regarded it as de- noting the lasting nature of the influence of a human being in, the world after, he himself had departed. In the minds of some thinkers this had been the *only kind of immortality which men ought to desire. This life, as we know it, gave -us an opportunity of making a contribu- tion th things; during its persistence we exerted in' influence, and that influence lived on in the memory and lives of others after we had gone. This was not, immortality as most men con- ceived the term. There was a second view which regarded it as a kind of re-absorption into the Deity. As God was the source of all being and the fount of all life, our lives —ere separated and distinct from the central life only for the time being, and at death wee to be received back again, taken up into the great ocean of life from which they came. This view involved the disappearance of separate identity. The' third view was that which asserted the' actual per- manence of personal consciousness, the lasting nature of the personality we possessed beyond the experience of physical death. An Enduring Personality.

"Now," continued the speaker, "if we have lost someone inexpressibly dear to us the supreme question of the human mind in its grief and. sorrow is. as to this third kind of immortality; whether the actual one we loved and knew is still living, whether we can reasonably expect to be reunited, whether we shall thily know each other in a future life. I do not think it is possible to believe that any other view than this underlies the teaching of the New. Testa- ment upon the question of the future life; the immortality. revealed' in Christ is alife.in which personality endures and is not interrupted by. the fact of death. lam convinced that the permanence of human affections points in the same direction, and the lasting power of human love for those departed must be regarded as a .God-implanted factor of life whiphe will find its answer and'itasatisfaction in a renewed fellow- ship with those now gone from our sight." Christ said to the penitent thief, "To-day . thou shalt be with Me in Paradise!" Let Faith fasten on the words "'Thou" and "Me," and they carried with them no uncertainty; they involved the survival of the .actual individuals :who talked together in, that hour when Love died ,upon • the tree and God redeemedd-a world: Or we. had the Simple-language of Christ when He spoke of death, "Let not your heart he troubled, In my Father's house are many mansions; if it wesre not so I would have told you: I go to prepare a place for you." If we used the language of Christ about the future life and called it a house we used a word which signified not only, an abiding place, but friends to welcome and hearts to cheer those who came to it at .the last.

The first step that should be taken for a fainting person is to place the body in a re- cumbent position either on a couch or bed or on the floor if necessary, keeping the head low. The next step is to loosen the clothing and especially all stays and bands, so as to give free action to the lungs. The third step is to open the windows wide and get the patient's head as near the window as passible so as to supply an abundance of fresh air: Bathing the foiehead and face with cad water will hasten recovery and, it is a safe procedure to adopt. As soon as the patient is able to swallow, administer sips of hot or cold water or equal parts of milk and water. .If recovery is slow it is a ,good thing to raise the feet and to massage' the chest in the region of the heart. The application of a cold compress to the left side of the chest is also a valuable means of relief. On no account place a pillow under the,head which would only 'serve to aggravate the condition.— Dr. A. B. Olsen, in November "Good Itealth." Cramp. •

The duration of the spasm of cramp and its intensity differ, in different people. Sorae .who apparently enjoy good health are subject to it throughout life from _slight causes, such as lying with the limbs in a strained position, the weight of the extremity alone causing, it would appear, sufficient pressure to interfere with its normal blood supply. Growing boys and 'girls and young people are prone to suffer from it, as well, as old thin people with little fat to relieve .the pressure in the muscles. Like some other affections of muscles, it may come on after a period of muscular rest and also during sleep when for any reason the fatigued muscle is brought into action. The calf muscles are most frequently affected, owing to pressure in the sitting position or bending the knees, though certain occupations cause its appear:- ance in the upper extremities. As 'a rule, cramp lasts a few mii.autes only, but it may last for days and sometimes even longer, and a noticeable feature is that when a muscle such as the calf is once affected with cramp such seizures are likely to return frequently. When it is extremely common, warm baths before bedtime are of value. Any gouty or rheumatic tendencies call for appropriate treatment. div.p: CHAT and GOSSIP.
By MARJORIE.
Permanent Green Leaves.

Botanists all over the world will derive in- terest and pleasure from a method lately dis- covered by means of which the green colouring matter in the leaves of trees and plants can be rendered permanent. Unfortunately the colours of° flowers are so fugitive and elusive, they cannot at present be 'fixed by this new method. Experiments in the future may, how- ever, discover how this can be done. The col- lections faded and colourless now, in museums, will gradually be changed for leaves that will retain their form and natural green for an in- definite period of time. The method is as simple as it is valuable. Plants so preserved may .be exposed to the sirong sunlight, for years, without detriment. Some beautiful specimens of green, red and brown seaweeds, have also been shown, in which the colours have been permanently fixed. For a very long time the problem of how to preserve the green colouring matter in leaves, has engaged the at- tention of chemists and botanists, but their endeavours have only recently been crowned with success.

div.head: HOW BASKETS WERE FIRST MADE.
div.p: HOW BASKETS WERE FIRST MADE.

One of tlie prettiest Indian stories tells bow the beautiful Indian baskets came to be *oven. They say that Shade told .the first Weaver to make a basket, and if you notice how the 14 hadows of the twigs and grasses interlace you will see how like basket work_ their shadows look. The Weaver thought for a long time, and finally gathered different kinds of grasses„ and-,began to weave them together. At last she finished a basket, and took it to the lake to-fill it with water but;, alas! the water ran out, .for the grasses'. leaked. Then she looked at the shadows again, and saw, how tightly they were interlaced, and what a pretty pat- tern they made, and knew she must weave a fight basket With a Pattern 'on it. • 'She felt very despairing, and sat 'by the lake looking into the water, and there she suddenly saw the most beautiful .pattern reflected where the, trees bent over, and / the sight made her so happy that she longed to weave it into a basket, and never thought again about tbe difficulty. So this time she went to the forest. and f6und the red cedar roots.. Then the Weaver began to work, and :after many 'days. the basket was finished. She took. it to. the lake, and dipped it full of water, but this.time the water stayed. -The basket was tight, and it had the. pattern on it that the Shade had taught her. div.head: "A BLOODY REVOUTION."
div.p: "A BLOODY REVOUTION."
Wesleyan Minister On Settling Of Capital And Labour Question.

In conception as allegorical as Bunya)i's "Pilgrim's Progress.," ti 'lectures' delivered by the Rev. Howard May, :of Inverness; at Bold- street Church on Thursday evening, was entitled, "New Age Junction—All Change." The reverend gentleman pictured the arrival of a nation at the junction of a railway', and in in. teresting detail analogised all sections of- the community. We. had all arrived 'at this stage, and many were Still at the junction, but at least five millions—all soldiers—had gone on and were' making progress in their own lives and ,for the nation 'by their devotion to what they considered right. No one respeoted a genuine Conscientious objector • more' than he himself, but of many it could be said that they. were canting humugs. He could not under- stand how any man could witness this national crisis and do nothing; and, moreover, if those be- yond military age were not doing "their bit" in some way or other they,too were shirkers. In their journey the Government, he said: were greatly hampered by that deliCately con- trived and wonderful implement, the political party machine, and he .wished a bomb would drop on it to-morrow. (Laughter; and, AP- plause.) Mr. May hoped that at the .cbnclnsion of the war we would not 'be °enthralled in militarism, for, if that were so our lads had died in vain. He himself was also against the mak- ing of our railwaymen and miners into.soldiers, and he appealed to his "audience to play their part in warding off industrial•conscription.•The question of capital and labour had also got to be solved, and if it were not done ,there was a bloody' revolution coming. Ire was glad to see signs, however, that an amicable Understanding was being aimed at by certain representatives of capital and labour, and he hoped their ideas would liatte •a happy effect, whereby after the war we should have five or ten years' unrivalled; prosperity. -

THE TURN OF THE CATS.

The EMPEROR WILLIAM, who has said some original and startling things in his time and has'not been guiltless of sending telegrams to KRUGER, is credited with having stated in the early part of the war that he would arm his last cat in defence of Germany before he would acknowledge defeat. In those days he was living in castles in air, in which the atmos- phere was governed by the supposed certainty of victory and the British Army was a con- temptible little organisation that was to be walked over. Well, we have ehanged all that. This week we have been so far removed from the contemptible stage, that we have, con- tray to all traditions, v ;taken an aggressive move, despite the winter mud, and adminis- tered the greatest defeat upon the Germans that they have sustained during the war in a like period. The result is that the Germans have realised that the cats may yet have to be mobilised. At all events, steps are to be taken to bring the whole man and woman power of Germany into the military machine —that machine that Was to crush all before it in a few short months so long ago as 1914. If Germany is recognising that every step must now be taken to avoid final disaster we must take the corresponding steps to neutralise all her efforts and make that disaster certain. Every ounce of strength must, and will, go into the scale against the enemy.

div.head: TRIP IN A GIG.
div.p: TRIP IN A GIG.
Broom Edge Publican Fined For Permitting Drunkenness.

Much interest was taken in a licensing case at Lymm Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, when Joseph Carless Gough, licensee of the Jai .- Thresher Hotel, Broom Edge, was fined two guineas and special costs and advocate's fee, for permitting drunkenness On --his premises, and James Shepherd, a horse dealer, of Bridgewater- 3treet, Lymm, was fined 10s. for, being drunk in charge of a horse and trap on the highway. Outlining the case, Mr. Caldecott, solicitor for the prosecution, said that on Friday after- the 13th October, Mr. Mort, the surveyor to the Lymm Urban District Copncil., was out •-cling, and in Penny Hill he saw Mr. Shep- ;ierd in a gig, leaning over the side. There was ,a,steam roller in the distance and, as the man in the gig was obviously drunk, Mr. Mort was afraid that the pony might jib. The police were standing slightly farther along the road, and he informed them of Shepherd's condition, which was that of being helplessly 'drunk. In the evening the police visited Mr. Gough, who admitted Mr. Shepherd had had three 'or . four whiskies, that when he went out of the- house he was not quite sober, and that he (Mr. Gough) trent' along the road with him in the trap for over a mile. . _ .

Alter giving evidence, Mr. Mort was asked by Mr. Hockin, of Manchester, who appeared for the defence, whether he had known Shepherd, who was seventy years of age, to have been drunk before. He replied, " No." Sergeant Davies,. P.C. Gauld and P.C. Ather- ton gave evidence to the effect that Shepherd wa.. helplessly drunk when they saw him in the gig. As he was searched at the Police Station he was unable to stand.

Mr. Irockin to Sergeant Davies: Mr. Shepherd, has a reputation for sobriety P—No. You have seen him drunk P—Yes,..:and have been called to his house in consequence of his conduct: Witness admitted that when the. defendant. said he had gone along the road with Shepherd,. besides saying the latter was not quite sober. but capable of driving, he also said Shepherd had been asking him to huy the pony, so he went with him to see how it shaped. Mr. Gough, in the witness box, deposed that ho sold Shepherd three small whiskies, and when be left the premises he was absolutely sober. He could not account for his being found drunk, as the prosecution stated. It was pos- sible that -the fresh air or the cigar he was smoking overcame him. The reason he (Gough) went with Shepherd was he wanted to test the pony's wind. • Other witnesess were called to say that when Shepherd was on the premises he did not show any signs of being drunk.

div.head: HIGH PRICES.
div.p: HIGH PRICES.
Are Our Farmers Playing The
Game?
PATRIOTIC FARMER'S VERSION.
By S.D.M.

My last article on this subject seems to have created quite: a sensation among a certain section of the farming community. During last week I was approached by an interested' party, who endeavoured to explain to me the actual reason for the outrageous price demanded at the present time for potatoes. Although his reasons may be quite right and perfectly just, I hope that he will forgive me if I am at all inclined n6t to agree with him. You will re- member how I explained that the scarcity of labour had nothing at all to do with it; although it was quite a password with them; how I told the farmers the reasons why , the Tribunals had given them the greatest con- sideration; how I attacked them and accused them of demanding an unfair price for their produce, the burden of which chiefly fell on the wives and dependants of our gallant lads who are sacrificing their all to keep the old flag flying. After all that, this particular party ventured to tell -me that the price demanded for potatoes at .the • present day was due entirely to patriotic reasons. You may 'agree with him if you like, but I, personally, decline to do so. He says that now the supply of potatoes from Belgium and other theatres of war is no longer ,obtainable,, it is up to us at home to make our supplies last as long as possible. High 'Price To Check Waste.

There is a lot.of waste in potatoes, he said, and that ought not to be. If people come. across a potato that does not happen to be of a moderate size they throw it at one side and will not .take the trouble to peel it. The Same thing applies when they come across a potato that happens to be a little hit bad. Such waste, he continued, is uncalled for, and at the present time is nothifig short of a scandal. Now, if these facts were absolutely true, I should feel inclined to grant them my sym- pathy, but I can hardly take them in. Fancy, for one minute, a soldier's wife going to her dealer and purchasing 51b. of potatoes, for which she pays 61d., and when she gets them home scrapping them because they di 4 not hap- pen to be of a moderate size. Imagine her doing that on the meagre allowance she is granted by the State. Why, I can almost see her scrubbing the potatoes so that she can boil them in their jackets to make them go further. If farmers want us to believe that these prices are due to patriotic reasons, then let them show it by giving half of their extra profits, to local war charities, for we all know that actions speak louder than .words. They will-still have a substantial extra. profit to put on one side for future emergencies, and will also have &clear conscience, with the knowledge that they have done their best to bring this terrible war to a successful issue. •

div.head: ‘A YU IN'S SPIIERE.
div.p: ‘A YU IN'S SPIIERE.
Should We Have A Parliament Of Women?

A very interesting discussion on "Women's Sphere" was held on Thursday evening in the Wesley Guild .Room. The champion of the women's cause., was Mr. E. England, who stated thAt man.' hs retardeA': the ,progress ,of the human race by his claim to superiority. Man based his supposition on the theory that he is physically stronger, but on this argument he himself will have to give way to the elephant, lion, tiger, &c., and even the despised donkey is physically stronger than man. Women's sphere is anywhere and everywhere in true co- operation with her partner, man. He went on to show,how women had succ‘eded in scholastic work, literature, art, sculpture, social, Red Cross, business, munitions, gardening, farming, &e., work, and home life, .though there were some 'spheres from which women up to the pre- sent had been prohibited—ministry, legislation, Stn., though it was obvious that before long women would have the vote in this country. He advocated a separate Parliament for women to settle the women's problems, and a Parlia- ment for men to settle the men's problems, and a joint Parliament to settle national affairs which affected the general community.- What is wanted' is a complete iiartnership with man, equality of opportunity in all things according to the capacity of the individual. As a result this would lead to- a better ordered social state without the chaos, as at present. It would also result in greater production and shorter hours, tend to the uplifting of humanity, joined hand in, hand together to work out problems and salvation,of the .human race. •

Mr. W. E. Plinston;.,.who spoke in the nega- tive, mentioned that women's truest sphete was in the home. speaking, of literature, he admitted 'that women, to a certain extent had done good work, but when: compared with such as Scott, Burns, Tennyson, Dickens, Shakes- peare, Ruskin, &c., they were certainly the in- ferior. In music all the great composers were men, and in commercial life the bulk of the work that. was being done by women had 'to be finished off by the men. In farming they were not a success,- and it was even said that educa- tion was suffering ,considerably owing to the dearth of male teachers.' -

• Mr. T. B. Duckworth also gave some inter- esting quotations from various writers, show- ing what they have said about women, illus- trations being taken from Shakespeare, George Herbert, Browning, Burns, Burke, Oliver W. Holmes, &c. The ladies, who were in the majority at the meeting, were given an opportunity of. support- ing their cause, but although they had such an excellent advocate in M. England, they did not rise to the occasion as one would have ex- pected, though an excellent speech was made by Miss M. Ward, other speakers being Mrs. Dakin and Mrs. Stewart.
The meeting. which was presided over by the Rev. A. J. Morton, was thoroughly enjoyed, being brimful of humour throughout.

div.head: DRIVER PERCY ROYSTON.
div.p: DRIVER PERCY ROYSTON.
Absent Churchwarden On The Life
For Young Fellows.

" Something like a letter," is an apt expres- sion regarding that which Driver Percy Royston has addressed from his training quarters to the Rev. J. Hirst, who is in charge of Christ Church, Padgate, where Driver Royston officiated as a warden 'before enlisting.

After saying how pleased he is to. hear that everything is going on so nicely in the old parish, the writer says:— " Army life is a great change for me, I can asskire you, but I .am, along with the rest of the boys, doing what I can to become proficient. You cannot be long in the service without being struck by the great bond of fellowship that exists amongst. the troops. Everyone is a pal, and what one man is short of another will try and assist him.

"We have 30 good fellowk in our, hut, and we are a happy 'family. Most of • them are married men, and, like myself, have the theughts of those whom they have left before them. It seems to me best 'not to think too much about old times, but to concentrate your mind on your present duties; otherwise you are apt to get discontented. As a driver in the R.F.A. most of my time is occupied on and among the horses. It is n fine sight to see us turn out, and there is no small amount of ex- citement when we gallop over the plains. We seldom get the same horse twice, and there is always an element of doubt as to what we are in for as regards its tricks, &c. If everything else fails I ought at least to make my way in some circus. Army life' is the life for young fellows, and though old men are to be made into young ones, you may be sure the 'time' occupied in the making is not exactly a picnic. 'We often say as a joke that we cannot understand the young fellows not coming up—the money is good, but not much of it. , "The inner man is well looked after, and there is no need for anyone to go short. If you feel you, want something extra, you can get it outside at reasonable prices. The troops here owe a great deal to such ,organisations as the Church of England Institute, the Y.M.C.A. and Salvation Army: These have large .huts, set apart scilely for soldiers, where refreshments can be obtained and papers and games are sup- plied. They are all bright spots and worthy objects for people to support "Will you please remember me to any who may ask after me? With my kindest thoughts, I remain, yours most sincerely, P. Roston."

The Superintendent explained that at 11.30 on Saturday morning, the 3rd of this month, a police constable, who was on special daty in the vicinity of Dallam, saw the women go in the dirsction of Dallam Farm. He saw them enter a field where potatoes were being gathered, after about 'half an hour, leave the field with a quantity of potatoes in their aprons. On Monday, in the Munitions Court, before Mr.. T. 'J. Ridgway, four young • men named Thomas .McGarry, Wm. Brady, Samuel Ellison and Thomas P. Breese, employed formerly as labourers by a. local firm of soap manufacturers applied for a.week's wages, which they claimed in lieu of notice, received on November 2nd. Ellison was not present,' but sent a'note to the Clerk, Mr. G. P. F. White. . McGarry, who gave evidence on behalf of himself and companions, stated that they were dismissed on November, 2nd by the Technical - Director.. Some nails were found in the soap, and the Director asked them if -they knew any- thing about it. Each of them said he knew nothing at all about it. The Director, replied, "If I can't find out who has done. it I will have to dismiss the whole lot of you." Between. thirty and forty worked in the same room. Mr. Ridgway: Had nails been put in th.e, soap?—Yes, I saw the nails in the soap. Is soap made in your room?—Yes. Did you put the nails in or any of you four —No, .none of, us knew, anything about it. I have no, idea who put in the' nails. You bare all -got certificates ?—Yes. Yoll have not got work?—Nó, sir, wanted to know what we were sacked for bfeliflolVeT we started.

Technical Director: On the morning of November 2nd, about 5.30, did not the foreman speak to you and three others for-having a con- cert together P---Yes. You ‘vere singing in the " peeling " room P-- Yes.

The Technical 'Director handed in a copy °t the firm's rules and sh,owed that there had been a wilful waste of time. The Manager said that wlen two of .the applicants, McGarry and Breese, came to him to reiterate their innocence of the nail incident. he made it abundantly clear to them, that they were not being dismissed for that. He told them that it was a grave coincidence that there was an attempt made to damage the machinery .on the morning that they were dismissed. He also said that any information they could give him with regara.to the nail incident that would lead to the detection of the guilty person or persons would be taken into account, and 'the firm would be ,prepared to consider their applications for reinstatement and subject to such punishment as they thought fit to impost' for the breach. of rules. The Technical Director said•that the men had been suspended early in the morning, pending- the Manager's arrival at the works. Shortly after nine o'clock a villainous attempt was made to damage the machinery by salting a box of soap with nails. The machine in question was the one on which these men had been work- ing. He admitted that he was distinctly biased by this second incident Mr. Ridgway: You have not discharged thou on the incident of the-nails? 4

. 'Crossing to the open window Blair looked down into the garden. There wa,3 Angelo, the Italian gardener, taking the diamond from the bush into which it had fallen when cast through the window by the indignant Esther. • _ .
"Hi, there, you!" called Blair, "don't take that, I am coming down for it." _ _

The gardener, who, like the rest of the servants, bore a sullen dislike to the whilorn friends who surrounded their master, growled an uniatidligible reply. Durand, who sensed that the diamond had been found, sprang from the rcom and nicele for the stairway with Blair beside him. They ran from the front of the house to the back, but the ,gardener picked up a heavy stake lying by the rose bush and kept them off.

"I take it to the boss," he said. Nor would he be shaken from his resolve. Durand and Blair, cursing his stubbornnea. escorted him back into the house and to Arthur. Vivian, realising the diamond was recovered, had •eeased her vixenish demands, and was again ilesort- ing to wiles and cajolement. But Arthur, shaken with shame and wholly unnerved that they should have deceived him as regards Esther's presence in the city, his shame augmented by the realisation that Esther knew now how he had fallen in his drug addiction, took the diamond and staggered from the room, with a few muttered thanks to the gardener. _ _ _ _ _ _ _

- Reaching his suite, he locked the diamond in an .ornate cabinet by the great window of his bed- room, and then, pacing up and down, fouklit the devil of drug desire for Esther's sake—and lost again. _

-The English lawyer, Smythe, a knieht in armour in all .sooth, escorted the shaken Esther to her hotel, having picked up the watching and waiting Quabba in front of the 'Powell mansion and taken him with them in his taxicab. _ . _

"I will see you safely back to Richmond," said Smythe, gently. "Your mother. von say, has re- covered, and you wish to return to her. "But what shall I do about Luke Lovell?" asked Bather. "All his life, except for the brief revolt— he now begs forgiveness for—he served my mother faithfully."

"I would 'suggest," said Smythe, " that our friend Quabba, here, stay behind us and see what he can do. He may secure L'ovell's release by lip- :pealing to Arthur Stanleigh." "I have no' faith "in Arthur now," sid Esther, wearily. "Ho has fallen into evil ways through associations."- But in her steadfast heart .Esther resolved to say nothing to Smythe now, nor Hagar later, regarding Arthur's drug habits. "Well," suggested the English lawyer, "our friend Qua,bba, can keep us posted, and we may be :able to take up the matter of endeavouring to ,Aecuro Lovell's release from this unjust incarcera- tion after we return to Richmond."
Quabba; who had always liked Luke, except for the quarrel between them at Luke's revolt, eagerly ,agreed to the plan, though he was loth to part, even -temporarily, from his mistress _ • _ _

_ The next day Esther. accompanied by Smythe, left Los Angeles for Richmond. Quabba, placed in funds by the lawyer, stayed behind.' Quabba was an Italian gipsy, and his new friend and com- patriot, the gardener at the Powell mansion, was at the train with him • when he made 'his 'respect- ful adieus to his young mistress and to Smythe. On the way back from the depot, the gardener, .deeming Quabba needed cheering, led him to the garden-restaurant, La Bella Napoli. It was a bumble place, an arboured resort frequented by Italian working people. Signora Solari made them welcome.

"She has no good looks," whispered Quabba,'s friend. "but you should see her daughter ..Rosa. Ah, Rosa is a charmer. and how she will ,smile at ioti if you pay for the better wine. You should see her." It was fated that Quebba was to see the ravish- ing Rosa. De Vaux. a lady killer to his way of thinking, had also seen the ravishing Rosa. She had smiled at Do \Tunic in passing, and he had fol- lowed her to 0,- garden La Bella Napoli. A citizen of the world, the dapper count, who spoke Italian charmingly, knew well how to ingratiate himself into the favour of the landlady's daughter and the lady. De Vaux ordered Chianti, on which there was a good profit. _ _ _ _ _

From-their-table in the garden Quabba and the Powell gardener noted all this, but kept their dis- tance, unseen and unnoticed by the languiAing De Va,ux. Fate was playing into the hands of Quabba. Cesare, the contractor, had joined Quitbba and his friend at their table in the corner. He had a griev- ance, the contractor. "Look you," he said. "I get a contract, a good contract, to fix a roof, and I can't get any of these lazzaroni to go on tbe work."

Questioned why by Quabba, Cesare shrugged his shoulders and said: "There are two reasons the loafers give me. One is that it is a non-union job, and the other is it. is work at the pris.on—and that they do not like. They fear the prison, maybe for good reasons.''
Quabba, sat erect. Tio prison? Litye was in the • prison.

"Me, observe me. Roofing! That was my trade," cried Quabba. "Angelo- here will tell you." Angelo, who knew nothing at all of the matter. swore that Quabba was the best ruotcr that had ever left Italy.

The following day Quabba waS at work at the roof, but he did not give the contractor satisfaction: " You a fine roofer," the contractor declared, scornfully. "You no good." Quabba shrugged his shoulders. and replied: "Ha, what you tink you get for this job, a jeweller?" • "All right. To-morrow I fire you, and hire the monkey you have. , He gotta more brains," and -the contractor spat in disgust, and threw down the loop of scaffold rores he was carrying and hobbled away.

In Richmond, at the Riverview sanatorium, Hagar had almost wholly recovered. The clot upon her brain caused by the cruel blow Blair had struck her had been absorbed. Her memory came back to her, but the death, after a stroke of paralysis, of Blair's mother and meditation during her con- valescence had broadened Hagar's gipsy nature to a disposition of forgiveness. The sorrow she had undergone in the disappointment Arthur, her pro- fligate son, had been to her, also chastened Hagar's proud spirit.

Through Esther's letter, she now knew that Arthur, in all his wealth and luxury, had sur- rounded himself with evil company, and that Blair and the adventuress, Vivian Marston, were among his familiars and parasites. Reunited at the sana- torium, Hagar and Esther embraced and wept when they spoke of Arthur.

"It is greed that has changed him," said Hagar, softly. " Money-greed—that was his father's curse." And Hagar's mind reverted to that dreadful night of physical and mental anguish when Arthur had been born to her and his unnatural father, the dead Matt Harding, had sold his new-born child to Colonel Stanleigh to further the family ambitions and family hatreds of the Stanleighs. "It was money-greed that led poor Luke Lovell to revolt and evil courses," continued Hagar. "I am happy to know that Luke is contrite of heart in all save for his present desire for vengeance on Arthur and his associates who have betrayed and imprisoned him ungenerously, as he thinks." "He is very bitter to them," murmured Esther. " IA asks your forgiveness, mother dear, and longs to return and serve you faithfully once again. But he will not be stirred from his determination to have vengeance."

"Vengeance is Mine, saith the Lord; I will re- pay." and from her heart was banished all hatred for those who had wronged her, even the wild Blair Stanleigh, who had struck her down cruelly and cowardly, and who now was among those who sur- rounded her own wild son, strangling his soul. " We will return home, to your home, my dear child, to Stanleigh Hall," whispered Hagar when she regained her composure. "There we will dis- cuss the plans "I have long meditated upon since my recovery, and in your absence. Perhaps this good friend will go with us and give us the benefit of his able counsel," and she turned to the sympa- thetic, eccentric English lawyer, who had accom- panied Esther from the West, and again thanked him brokenly for his kindness to and his protection of Esther.

Durand, the pseudo doctor, was becoming im- patient,_ and decided to force matters. "I want quicker action,"- he said to Vivian. "There is money and the diamond in the safe in Powell's room, and I am going to get it. We are fooling away our time as vie are going on."

The impression was gradually growing upon Arthur that he was being imposed upon, and he felt that he was strong enough to dispense with Durand, and, handing him a substantial cheque, summoned sufficient courage to tell him so. Now, if ever, the King of Diamonds must act, and he proposed that they should have one more evening at cards. Arthur agreed, and that night, while the game was at its height, Durand dropped a sleeping powder into Arthur's glass. The game broke up owing to the sleepy languor of the host, who was led away by Blair.
"Now young woman. you listen to me," said Durand to Vivian, when they were left alone. "I'll take the diamond to-night. I know enough to gaol the rest • of you if you betray me."

Nivian, however, took that risk -and.. betrayed Durand to Blair. Hiding in her room after mid- night. Blair and Vivian heard Durand creep down the hail. They gave him time to enter and works in the room of the drugged and unconscious Master, of the house. Then on noiseless feet the desperate Blair stole in upon the King of Diamonds. Unseen, unheard, Blair crept behind Durand in the semi- darkness of Arthur's room as he prized open the cabinet. Without a word Blair dealt him a blow with all his strength with the loaded stick he car- ried. The blow glanced, and Durand, no mean antagonist even for the stalwart Blair, closed in upon his assailant. They cursed and swayed and struggled. Blair, held too closely by Durand to give full swing to his deadly weapon, rained blow. after blow upon Durand at short range. Arthur was roused by the struggle .from his drugged sleep, and rose 'dazed yet wide-eyed from his bed. Vivian, in a tremor of anxiety in the door- way, switched on the lights full and bright. At the light Blair rose to a frenzy of murderous activity. He seized Durand by the throat, his weapon-arm now free, and brought the stick down with sickening force upon the skull of the bleeding Durand, and then cast the battered King of Dia- monds from him with a mighty effort. Back, thine like a sack, the thief, weak and stunned, fell against the low, wide window, and through it down to the lawn below, striking full upon his head, breaking his neck. He had carried with him to his death, clutched with a grip Blair could not loosen, the Diamond from the Sky.

As Durand lay broken and dead Upon the ground a figure crouched over him in the shadow. A hand wrested the diamond from the relaxing grasp of the dead swindler. There was a thudding of hur- ried feet across the lawn, and the man was gone, and with him the fatal gen. (To be continued.)

The game opened at a fast pace, with Warritie-• ton having the best of matters. Tranter broke away with a splendid dribble, but with practically an open field knocked on. From the scrummage the Recs.' forwards forced play to the half-way line, but fine passing by the Warrington backs drove them back. Some scrambling play took place "near the line, and Matthews picked the ball up and ran over for Warrington, Dainteth failing to convert. On resuming, the Recs. forced matters, and a for- ward rush 'looked. dangerous for the, visitors, until Tranter picked up and cleared. The home team. however, returned to the attack, and through the instrumentality of the threequarter backs, headed by M'Conms and Glover, reached the Warrington line. Here scrummaging took place, but the ball came out to the Warrington halves and was cleared. The forwards followed up at top speed, and the ball was forced out of play at the three- quarter line. From the resulting scrimmage Brookes received and passed to Tranter, who was tackled only, a few yards from the line. A fine run by Bowen relieved the danger, and that player's effort being seconded by Greenall and Marr, the War- rington quarters were reached. The stay in this proximity, however, was of short duration, for clever work by Young and Douglas. saw the home line again menaced. Glover was tackled under the home posts, and, failing to play the ball, was penalised. Dainteth took the kick and made War- rington's total into five points. div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.

In our last notes we were ccnimenting on secre- taries holding their matches earlier on in the season, especially in canals, and now we have a poster to hand advertising a match to be held November 26th in the waters of the Pearson and Knowles Angling Society (kindly lent for the occa- sion), near Moss Collieries, Ince, for prizes rang- ing from £5 downwards. Northern Anglers' com- petition rules will be observed. The draw will be, at Moss Bridge, Leeds and Liverpool Canal (Leigh btanch), at 10.15 a.m.; time of fishing, two hours. The match is in aid of Ince Soldiers' and Sailors' Comforts Fund. Whether they will receive many entries from the Warrington district or not I am not prepared to say. For those who have machines it is quite handy. Any further information re- quired by locals may be got from the secretary, G. W. Clough, 2,4l3urg,ess-street, Lower Ince. THE WEAVER CONTEST. •

The contest held at Newbridge last Sunday week between six selected from Manchester and district and six from Warrington, resulted in an easy win for Manchester. Warrington men were at a disad- vantage, as the contest was rather late for our style of fishing the Weaver. Warringtonians believe in maggot and feeder for Quick fishing; the Manchester men place more faith in their ground bait, as their matches are of longer duration. The weather being cold and wet. it was all to the advantage of the Manchester team. F. Smith, the crack from Sale, was an eaey rfirst in his team, and F. Jolley, our local champion, was easily first in the Warrington team. After the first hour it was plainly seen that Manchester would win unless our locals adopted some method that would get a better class of fish, and that is Most unlikely in the Weaver. We trust this kind of contest fishing will continue in the shape of a League. Most of the competitors in the above match were in favour of such a scheme, and the next move would be a meeting of secre- taries, either in Manchester, Warrington, or North- wich, to get the matter moving. Warrington has already a scheme to put forward if ever there is such a meeting called.

The home team made the first dangerous attack, but the visitors' defence gradually relieved their lines, and play was taken to the home quarters, where the defence were hard pressed. The home goalkeeper had to handle three times in quick suc- cession, and Heesom hit the woodwork twice with good shots. The siege was eventually raised, and Pearson, gaining possession, transferred to the opposite end, and from his centre Glover scored the first goal after twenty-five minutes' play. After this reverse the visitors played more determinedly, and Warburton scored an off-side goal. Still keep- ing up the pressure a penalty kick was given against Thomasson for hands. Green took the kick and made no mistake, making the scores equal. Half-time score: One goal each.

The second portion opened very ken, and in favour of the visitors, but the home backs played a great game. Sankey was carefully watching Green, the visitors' centre-forward. The home forwards' began to show more combination and got to close quarters with the visitors' backs. A penalty kick being awarded, Pearson took the kick and gained the lead for the home team. The game now assumed a ding-dong character, and occasionally of a rough nature, which' brought the referee in con- flict with the players, and free kicks were fre- quent. Towards the close of play the visitors gained a corner kick, and the ball was well placed by Ileesom, and Warburton made the scores equal with a crowd of players in the goalmouth. Immediately after the final whistle blew, and the score was: Penketh Juniors, 2 goals; Latchford Recs., 2 goals.

This gave relief to the visitors' defence, and then some keen ex- changes were witnessed in midfield. Owing to the excitement of the players the game became very erratic, and mis-kicking was frequent, but the re- spective goalkeepers were not severely tested. The interval arrived without any scores being regis- tered.

On resuming, the home forwards made a raid on the visitors' citadel, but found Johnson. Bell and Hughes very much alert, and they were driven back to midfield. Then the visitors became the aggres- sors and forced a couple of corner kicks, upon which they failed to improve. The game was again being contested in midfield for a while, with little advantage to either team. As the final stage was being entered upon the home team renewed their efforts. Owing to keen play the visitors' ,backs became unsteady in their clearances, and Martin, taking advantage of a mis-kick, rushed between the backs and scored for the heme team. In the few minutes that remained to play the visitors made desperate efforts .to equalise, but failed to make any impression on the home defence. Final score: Widnes Juniors, 1 goal; Highfield Juniors, nil.

Orford paid their first visit to Thelwall-lane to meet the Grappenhall lads. In the second half the home team soon showed signs of distress, and at, the close of play they had to acknow- ledge defeat by three clear goals. Chisholm and Buckley were the most dan- gerous forwards for the Juniors, and Gibson and Doughty were very safe in the back positions.

div.head: Student F3r Latchford Baptists.
div.p: Student F3r Latchford Baptists.

We have pleasure in announcing two interest- ing appointments in the Latchford area. The Ifev. H. B. Firth having resigned from the vicariate of St. James' (Latchford), the Rev. E. Milner Swift, of Rock Ferry, has been appointed his successor. Mr. D. J. Lewis, a student at Manchester Baptist College, has acceptor the pastorate of Wash-lan Baptist Church.

div.head: St. James'.
div.p: St. James'.

Mr: Swift is no stranger to Warrington, for from 1908 to 1911 he acted as curate in the parish in which he has just been appointed vicar by the Rev. H. V. Pigot, rector of Grappenhall, who is the patroneof the living. His associations with St. James' we remember very vividly, and his return to the scene of his past labours is viewed with the greatest pleasure by the parishioners, now that they are becoming reconciled to the forthcofning departure of the Rev. H. B. Firth, Born in 1882, the new vicar was first educated at Wallasey, Grammar School. The rev, gentle- man is a graduate of two Universities—the Royal, Dublin, and the Queen's, Belfast and gained his M.A.. degree last year at the latter' University. On leaving St. James' in 1911 he went to St. Peter's Church, Crewe, where he acted as curate-in-charge until 1915, when he was inducted .as vicar of St. Peter's Church, Rock Ferry. He is expected at Wal-rington at the end of the year.

div.head: Wash-lane Baptist.
div.p: Wash-lane Baptist.

A comparatively young man and still a student at the Manchester Baptist College, Mr. David John Lewis first made .acquaintance with the Wash-lane Baptist Church during the Summer. Monthly visits to the Sunday services have im- pressed the people, and it was a hearty invita- tion, which he has accepted. His term at col-

div.head: 3iR. D. J. LEWIS.
div.p: 3iR. D. J. LEWIS.

-lege not expiring until July, he will not, how- ever, be seen in charge until then, but an ar- rangement ha 4 been made whereby he will take the services on one Sunday each month. It is a happy circumstance that he will conduct the services on the last Sunday of the year and the first in the New Year. Mr. Lewis will come to his new charge with some experience of pastoral work, for during his term in college he has had two "station pastorates," at Hall-street and Great Clowes. -street, Broughton. Son of the Council Surveyor at Knighton, Radnorshire, he was in business before, entering college, imit all his spare time was devoted to the study and practice of what was to become his life work. Active in the local church, he was also superin- tendent of the Morning school at Commercial- road, Newport (Mon.), and secretary of the Sunday school at Knighton.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
TOULMI \ -FLEMING.

On Thursday afternoon an attractive wedding took place in Wycliffe Congregational Church, When the conttaating parties' were Mr. George Charles Parker Toulinin, son' of Mrs. Toulmin, Grappenhall-road, Latchford, and Miss Lucy Fleming, daughter of Mr. Louis Fleming,- St. Mary-street, Latchford. There was a large at- tendance at the church, and the ceremony was performed by the Rev. T. T. James. The bride, who was given away by her father, ware a reSs of white silk crepe de chene trimmed with orange blossom and handsome embroidered veil lent. by her cousin (Mrs. G. Cox). She carried 'a shower bouquet of white chrysanthemums and lilies. The bridesmaids were the Misses Emma, Annie and Clara Fleming, sisters of the bride, the first being dressed in pink eoleine and the latter two in blue eoleine, and all carried showe..• bouquets of pink carnations. Driver A. Flem- ing, Royal Engineers, brother of the bridegroom, acted as best man, and Private A. Critchley, R.W.F., brother-in-law of the bride, and Mr. W. Fleming, brother of the bridegroom, were groomsmen. lir. W. H. Payton presided at the organ. The hymn was "ta perfect love," and Mendelssohn's Wedding March was played. The reception, followed by a whist drive and dance; was at Atkinson's Cafe.. The happy couple are spending their honeyigoon• in Bux- ton, the bride's going away costunle being navy blue with black velour hat and black furs. Many handsome presents were 'received. Mr. Toulmin is secretary to the Junior Liberal Association.

div.head: FARRINGTON-HASSALL
div.p: FARRINGTON-HASSALL

• On Saturday a pretty and -interesting weddin,,,, took place at the Church of the Sacred Heart, Warrington, the bridegroom being Mr. William Farrington (Engine Room Artificer, R.N.), elder son of Mr. and Mrs. M. The .bridegroom joined the Navy a year and eight months ago, and for the past 16 months has been serving on a torpedo destroyer in the North Sea. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. The bridesmaids were Miss Annie Farrington and Miss Hilda Hassall, sisters respectively of the contracting parties. Thcy each wore signet rings, presents from the bri4e- groom. The Bride wore silk crepe de chine, trimmed with lace, and a veil with wreath of orange blossoms. She Carried a sheaf of Madonna lilies. Miss Annie Farrington was attired in embroidered silk . voile with black and white hat to match, and Miss Hassall in a dress costume of champagne 'silk crepe •de chine .. with large black .picture hat. After the ceremony a reception was .held at the Lion Hotel, Bridge-street. There was, a very large number of wedding presents.

div.head: MILITARY TRIBUNALS.
div.p: MILITARY TRIBUNALS.
SUBSTITUTION.
U The New Men Are Not Efficient ?

. At yesterday's Tribunal in the Town Hall Mr. F. Wright, builder, appealed on behalf of an employe, aged 3.5 years and married. The man, a bricklayer by trade, had been engaged in the, repair of a great amount of property on an estate. Prior to the war applicant had six men engaged on this work,, and had now only' this man. The other five- were with the Forces, and two of them had left since the last hearing of his application. _
The Chairman said there was a new scheme as regards substitution. This man would be called up with the object of getting a substitute. Mr. Wright could say if the substitute sent was not efficient.
Mr. Wright said it was a most difficult thing to find a man to do the different classes of work this man did. lie was the Most handy man,he had in that direction that he knew of. "

The Chairman replied that under the new scheme the Tribunal had to act, but applicant would have a voice in -the matter 'in this way: If the substitute supplied was not to his satis- faction he could object, and if his objection was valid it would hold good. Captain Heaton said the substitution would not be made by the-military, but through the Employment Exchaages. Mr. Wright said it woad be most difficult to replace this man. •• ; ' Dr. Joseph: You nfay not.get a man so effi- cient for your purpose, .but`that will be your sacrifice.

div.head: Mainspring.
div.p: The Mainspring.

Mr. C. H. Unsworth, solicitor, applied on behalf of Melbourne, Ltd., for, a furnaceman, aged forty years and having four children. The man had already been granted three months' exemption, and had been told that he could apply again. "We can't get another man," de- clared Mr. Unsworth, "and he, being a furnace- man, is the mainspring of the concern" Conditional exemption was granted.

div.head: RURAL TRIBUNAL.
div.p: RURAL TRIBUNAL.
Big Review Of Agricultural Exemptions Pending.

Further appeals for exemption on behalf of their sons, young unmarried men, were made by farmers at Wednesday's . meeting of the Rural Military Tribunal. • • .... In one case further exemption was given until April Ist, but the .majority were extended to January Ist, subject to substitution by the mili- tary authorities. - Mr. Furness, military representative, ex- plained that the men who, would be offered in substitution .would be 'drawn from classes C 2 and Ca, men discharged from the Army, and men used to agricultural work. At the close of the list Mr. Furness made an application for review in quite a number of agricultural cases. He proposed to bring them up in small batches on Wednesday afternoons week after week, so as to get them settled before the Ist January. Objected to Substitutes.

An applicant, who has a market garden at Fearnhead, appealed for exemption for his son, a young man, 23 years of age. In reply to the Military Representative, he said his daughter is a typist on. the Cheshire Lines Railwr.y, and was not 'fit to do any farm work. Asked, if a substitute, were provided; whether he 'would let his son go, applicant said decisively, "I won't take a substitute."

Rev. A. M. Mitchell: Supposing the Govern- ment says it must be so, or the military authorf- ties say it must be so? Applicant: I say no, I cannot. I would have to give the place up. Exemption, with substitution clause, granted until Ist January. A Burtonwood farmer asked for exemption for his son, 21 years of age, unmarried. Military Representative: Are cirou prepared, to take a substitute?
Applicant: I don't want a substitute. Will you he content with a'substitute?—Yes, if he suits. (Laughter.)

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S AMUSEMENTS.

For next week at the Palace and Hippodrome we are promised Wilf Burnand in his famous character studies; Jack Win and Nora Windle in a breezy burlesque, "Railway Revelations"; and Bob Morrison, Scottish comedian. Dancing will be represented by the Four Carltons, and artistic athletic perfection by Les Altos. J. E. Sutton and a piano suggests an attractive turn, and Fitz-Allen with a number of burlesque novelty songs is sure to have a good reception.

One of the most successful plays of modern times is to be produced, at the Royal Court Theatre next week: It is entitled "The Man who Stayed at Rome," and is full of ,the war ele- ment, much more interesting and novel than other plays of the kind we have seen. Who the "man who stayed at home" is we shall not say, but that it is a " Spy " play will give a stimulus to curiosity—and unless you know you have probably come to the wrong conclusion. The play is being presented by a splendid com- pany, and patrons may be assured of a grayd entertainment and much enlightenment.

At the Star Kinema House, Church-street, a place at which we can generally see fine topical films, we have had this week a fine picture of the King with his advanced Army on the Somme. Now we are having "The Moonstone." Next week we are to have "The Sales Lady" during the first half, and "Merely Mary Ann," ",Scenes of the Wrecked ZepPelin at Potter's Bar," and a Charlie Chaplin " scream " during the latter half.
